zutempo

Overview

Dates and times are hard to get right. A day is not always 24 hours, one month after 31 January is not a date, a clock time can happen twice or not at all, and the same moment is a different date in Tokyo than in New York. Most code gets these cases right by accident, or not at all.

Temporal is JavaScript’s answer: a date and time API designed by the committee that standardises the language, specified to the last nanosecond and tested by thousands of conformance tests. zutempo brings Temporal to R.

  • The right type for each job. A plain_date() is a date on a calendar, a plain_time() a time on a wall clock, an instant() an exact moment, a zoned_date_time() a moment in a time zone, and a duration() an amount of time. Each does what it says, and never silently becomes another.

  • Arithmetic you can trust. Adding a month, a day or 24 hours each mean what they should, across month ends, leap years and clock changes, and the ambiguous cases ask you how to resolve them instead of guessing.

  • The same answers everywhere. zutempo follows the Temporal specification operation by operation, so a result in R is the result in a browser or in Node. It is checked against test262, the specification’s own conformance suite.

  • At home in R. Values are vectors with NA, fit in data frames, convert to and from Date and POSIXct, and read time zones from the same database base R uses. The engine is in C, with no runtime dependencies.

Installation

zutempo is not on CRAN yet. You can install the development version from GitHub:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zutempo")

Usage 

library(zutempo)

A team meets every day at 9:30 in New York. Clocks go forward on the night of 7 March, so the next meeting is one day later, but only 23 hours later:

meeting <- zoned_date_time("2026-03-07T09:30[America/New_York]")
temporal_add(meeting, "P1D")
#> <zutempo_zoned_date_time[1]>
#> [1] 2026-03-08T09:30:00-04:00[America/New_York]
temporal_until(meeting, temporal_add(meeting, "P1D"))
#> <zutempo_duration[1]>
#> [1] PT23H

Where is everyone else at that moment?

temporal_with_time_zone(meeting, c("Europe/Lisbon", "Asia/Tokyo"))
#> <zutempo_zoned_date_time[2]>
#> [1] 2026-03-07T14:30:00+00:00[Europe/Lisbon]
#> [2] 2026-03-07T23:30:00+09:00[Asia/Tokyo]

Calendar arithmetic knows that months have different lengths:

due <- plain_date(c("2026-01-31", "2026-03-31", "2026-05-15"))
temporal_add(due, "P1M")
#> <zutempo_plain_date[3]>
#> [1] 2026-02-28 2026-04-30 2026-06-15
temporal_until(plain_date("2026-01-31"), "2026-12-25", largest_unit = "month")
#> <zutempo_duration[1]>
#> [1] P10M25D

And durations are values you can round, compare and total:

temporal_round(duration(minutes = 200), largest_unit = "hour")
#> <zutempo_duration[1]>
#> [1] PT3H20M
duration("PT90M") < duration("PT2H")
#> [1] TRUE
temporal_total(duration("P1M"), "day", relative_to = "2026-02-01")
#> [1] 28

Every function follows one naming rule: a Temporal type is a constructor (plain_date()), a method is temporal_ and its name (temporal_add()), and a property is a function of its name (year(), hours_in_day()). If you know Temporal, you already know zutempo.

Acknowledgements

zutempo is an implementation of the work of the TC39 Temporal champions, who designed the API and wrote its specification and its test262 tests. temporal-polyfill is the reference zutempo is checked against, and time zones come from the IANA time zone database. lubridate and clock showed how much R users care about getting dates and times right.
